newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland denies plans major spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Finland denies plans major spending cuts.

text.p: Finland's leaders on Thursday denied a report they were lining up swingeing spending cuts because sharp foreign exchange moves were jeopardising the country's bid to join Europe's single currency.
"There is no list of cuts that someone would have made and that for instance I would have in my pocket," Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen told a news conference.
He was asked about a report in daily Helsingin Sanomat that the finance ministry was planning new spending cuts, to eliminate the country's budget deficit next year if necessary.
The report said dollar and sterling strength was swelling the value of state debt, and that may threaten Finland's chances to meet the debt criterion for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Finland's total state debt at 428 billion markka ($76.1 billion) at end-July was over 70 percent of gross domestic product, but the finance ministry says the total measured for EMU purposes will be just under the 60 percent EMU ceiling this year.
Finance minister Sauli Niinisto said recent appreciation in the currencies had some effect on Finland's debt as measured by the EMU criteria, but this was not of major significance.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, he added that he believed the EMU debt was already below the 60 percent ceiling.
The finance ministry has come under heavy political fire by proposing extra cuts in next year's budget deficit, to 17 billion markka from an earlier planned 21 billion.
Total budget spending would be 188 billion markka.
Lipponen also said this year's deficit would be smaller than an earlier projected 26 billion markka.
